name: Pipeline & Backdoor
windOffshore: SE (surfnerd wind exposure E - S, "Offshore from SE"); SE (surfnerd guide text: "southeast (SE) offshore wind"); Southeast, East-southeast (surf-forecast); South (wannasurf)
tide: Low, Mid, High (surfnerd); Good surf at all stages of the tide. (surf-forecast)
bottom: Uneven Reef (surfnerd); Reef (coral, sharp rocks etc..) (wannasurf); Reef (coral, sharp rocks etc..) (wannasurf)
season: Autumn, Winter, Spring (surfnerd); Winter, most often January (surf-forecast)
notes: Surfnerd overview: Pipeline & Backdoor is the most famous wave on the planet, a heaving barrel that detonates over an uneven lava-slab reef only about 80 metres off Ehukai Beach Park on Oahu's North Shore. It's really two waves sharing one peak: Pipeline, the legendary left, and Backdoor, the super-hollow right that funnels across the shallow reef toward Off-The-Wall. Outer reefs refract and focus arriving swell onto the inside reef, so a wave that looks absent on a flat day can come roaring back to life when the right swell shows up. It's rated among the best waves in the world. Skill (surfnerd): Expert. Surf-forecast Pipeline_1: "Pipeline in Oahu is an exposed reef break that has fairly consistent surf, although summer tends to be mostly flat. The best wind direction is from the southeast. Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the best swell direction is from the west northwest. Often Crowded. Watch out for rocks and locals." Surf-forecast Backdoor-5: "Backdoor in Oahu is an exposed reef break that has quite reliable surf, although summer tends to be mostly flat. Works best in offshore winds from the southeast. Clean groundswells prevail and the ideal swell angle is from the northwest. A popular wave that can get growded. Watch out for - Rocks." Surf-forecast Banzai-Pipelines-and-Backdoor: "Banzai Pipelines and Backdoor in Oahu is an exposed reef break that has quite reliable surf, although summer tends to be mostly flat. Offshore winds are from the east southeast. Groundswells more frequent than windswells and the best swell direction is from the northwest. Reef breaks provide lefts and rights. Good surf at all stages of the tide. Often Crowded. Beware of rips and rocks." Wannasurf pipeline: quality Totally Epic; experience Pros or kamikaze only...; wave Reef-coral, Left; swell size Starts working at 1.0m-1.5m / 3ft-5ft and holds up to 4m+ / 12ft; crowd weekday Crowded, weekend Ultra crowded. Wannasurf backdoor: quality Totally Epic; experience Experienced surfers; wave Reef-coral, Right; swell size Starts working at 1.5m-2m /5ft-6ft and holds up to 5m / 16 ft and over; crowd weekday Crowded, weekend Ultra crowded. Access (surfnerd): Ehukai Beach Park sits right in front of the break, with a car park offering free parking plus roadside parking, though spaces fill fast when the surf is good. Facilities include restrooms, showers, and lifeguards on the beach. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Pipeline_1 0.4 km, surf-forecast Backdoor-5 0.3 km, surf-forecast Banzai-Pipelines-and-Backdoor 1.9 km, wannasurf pipeline 0.4 km, wannasurf backdoor 0.3 km.

hazards: Expect long rides, lots of paddling, and plenty of moving water, along with long hold-downs and real consequences when a big set catches you inside. (surfnerd)
season: Autumn, Winter, Spring (surfnerd); Winter, most often January (surf-forecast)
notes: Surfnerd overview: Sunset isn't one wave but a whole arena of sections spread across a huge playing field of uneven reef. It's a waterman's wave, where open-ocean power unloads and surfers swap equipment and adjust their approach to suit the reef's wide variability and moody nature. The zone runs from Val's Reef and the Inside Bowl to the West Peak, The Point, and Backyards, each section breaking differently depending on the day. Both lefts and rights show up, and the water is clean, clear, and blue. Skill (surfnerd): Expert. Surf-forecast Sunset_1: "Sunset in Oahu is an exposed reef break that has very reliable surf, although summer tends to be mostly flat. The best wind direction is from the south southeast. Groundswells more frequent than windswells and the best swell direction is from the northwest. Both left and right reef breaks. It very rarely gets crowded here. Beware of rocks and locals." Surf-forecast Sunset-Point-Vals-Reef: "Sunset Point/Vals Reef in Oahu is an exposed reef break that is often working, although summer tends to be mostly flat. Offshore winds are from the south southeast. Groundswells are more common than windswells and the ideal swell angle is from the northwest. There is a right hand reef break. When it's working here, it can get crowded. Beware of rocks and locals." Wannasurf sunset_beach: quality Totally Epic; experience Experienced surfers; wave Reef-rocky, Right; swell size Starts working at 1.0m-1.5m / 3ft-5ft and holds up to 5m / 16 ft and over; crowd weekday Crowded, weekend Crowded. Access (surfnerd): Getting in is easy, with public parking along Kam Highway right at Sunset Beach and roadside parking where authorized. There's a car park with free parking, plus restrooms and a lifeguard on hand. Because the outer waters are so deep, the Bay can look deceptively calm early in a big swell before the energy pours in and it turns into a massive washing machine, with water flooding in along the sides and a strong rip pulling out through the center. (surfnerd)
season: Autumn, Winter, Spring (surfnerd); Winter, most often January (surf-forecast)
notes: Surfnerd overview: Waimea Bay is the benchmark big-wave spot on Hawaii's North Shore, a right-hander that breaks over uneven reef and has long served as a proving ground for big-wave surfers. Deep, clear outer water lets swell arrive suddenly and trip on the lava ledge off the north point, producing the famous near-freefall Waimea takeoff, a fat shoulder, and a long race to the channel. It only comes to life on serious swells, and when it does every wave carries real consequence. Skill (surfnerd): Expert. The south side is usually the pick, though the north side has produced its share of memorable days. It can flip overnight from a closed-out, wishy-washy mushburger to a sand-sucking run of barrels, yet through all of that it stays remarkably consistent, both consistently rideable and consistently packed.

Every so often a right peels down the north side of the jetty into the estuary, running long and fast like a point wave.

It peels both left and right, and the ends of the battered jetties can get dredgy depending on where the sand has piled up.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Wabasso is a heavy beach shorebreak along Vero's shoreline, where waves stand up and dump thick right on the sand over a mostly sand bottom with some reef just off the beach. It is a bit of a rarity, but when the swell and tide line up it turns on, throwing punchy, board-snapping waves through a short, concentrated peak. When everywhere else is onshore and blown out, this is often the spot to hit, since the ridge of deep water and offshore reefs near shore clean the swell up before it explodes on the beach.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Wabasso in North Florida is an exposed beach break. Winter is the favoured time of year for surfing here. The best wind direction is from the southwest. Windswells and groundswells in equal measure and the best swell direction is from the north northeast. The beach break offers both left and right hand waves. Best around high tide. When it's working here, it can get crowded. Watch out for rips and sharks.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Walton Rocks is a beach break that some locals still call Power Plant, after the large nuclear plant sitting directly behind the pristine foreshore. The waves break over sand, but scattered dead coral and sponge reef formations help shape some sweet peaks along this stretch of coast, throwing up both lefts and rights. One nice quirk: cooling water discharged from the reactor feeds a warm current into the lineup, a welcome bonus for less hardy surfers in winter.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Walton Rocks is one of the many small coastal parks on South Hutchinson Island, fronting a shallow rock reef. It's a fickle spot that only comes together a few times a year, but when it does a powerful, well-tapered left peels down the reef. It earns a good rating on its day, even if the surf is more often weak and prone to sectioning.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Walton Rocks(Power Plant) in North Florida is an exposed beach and reef break that has very consistent surf, although summer tends to be mostly flat. Offshore winds blow from the southwest. Tends to receive a mix of groundswells and windswells and the best swell direction is from the northeast. Reef breaks provide lefts and rights. Best around low tide. It's sometimes crowded here. Hazards include sharks,nuclear power station nearby.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Waves and Salvo are neighboring stretches of Outer Banks beachbreak just south of Rodanthe, breaking over sand with both lefts and rights. The sandbars shift constantly here, so checking a few peaks to see how the sand looks is part of the routine, and when the banks line up they can serve up some of the most playful sandbars of the summer.

guideSummary.surfnerd: West End sits at the far tip of Jones Beach on Long Island, a sand-bottom jetty wave that peels right. It has been insanely fickle since the jetty was rebuilt, turning off for years at a time before reemerging for one shining season, so timing matters more here than at most spots. When it lines up it throws occasional right wedges and can get really fun on the right swell.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Wild Dunes is essentially one wide, flat, long beach breaking over sand. It picks up pretty much any swell going, and can turn juicy during a hurricane, though those days come with long, tough paddles out. At the far north end of the island, inside the Wild Dunes resort, sits a sandspit peak known as Charlie's that fires on solid northeast and east windswells.
